anchor: The woods decay, the woods decay
title: Tithonus: myth, date and companion poem
short: Begun in 1833 as 'Tithon', a companion to 'Ulysses'; revised in 1859 and published in the Cornhill Magazine, February 1860.
body: Tithonus, a Trojan prince, was loved by Eos (Aurora), goddess of the dawn. She obtained immortality for him but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he aged without end. Tennyson began the poem as 'Tithon' in 1833, in the months after Arthur Hallam's death, as a pendant to 'Ulysses': where Ulysses longs to go on, Tithonus longs only to end. When Thackeray asked him for a contribution to the new Cornhill Magazine, Tennyson revised the old draft (finishing it in November 1859) and it appeared in February 1860. RPO records the family tradition that his sister Emily, Hallam's fiancee, prompted it through her grief. It is a dramatic monologue in blank verse addressed to the goddess at dawn.

title: the opening cadence
short: Four end-stopped lines, each describing a natural ending, set against the speaker who cannot end.
body: The poem opens with a dying fall: woods decay and fall, vapours weep their burden to the ground, man tills the field and then 'lies beneath' it, the swan dies 'after many a summer'. Each line completes a natural cycle, and the repetition 'the woods decay, the woods decay' makes the rhythm itself sound like slow decline. Line 5 then breaks the pattern: 'Me only cruel immortality / Consumes', with the emphatic object pronoun placed first. The whole poem is built on this contrast between natural mortality and Tithonus's unnatural exception. Aldous Huxley took the title of his novel After Many a Summer (1939) from line 4.

title: burthen
short: Archaic form of 'burden': the load of moisture the mists drop as rain; the word also meant a song's refrain.
body: 'Burthen' is an older spelling of 'burden', a load (Old English byrthen). The vapours 'weep' their load of water to the ground, a personification that makes nature itself mourn. The OED also records 'burden' in the sense of the refrain or recurring theme of a song, and the opening lines do work like a refrain, repeating the idea of falling and ending.

title: after many a summer dies the swan
short: Swans were proverbially long-lived; even they die at last, and their dying was associated with song.
body: Swans were believed to live very long, so the line chooses the longest-lived creature to make the point that every life has its term. The swan was also traditionally said to sing before death: in Plato's Phaedo Socrates says swans sing most beautifully when they know they are about to die, out of gladness at going to the god they serve (Phaedo 84e-85b). Tithonus's whole speech is in a sense a swan-song he is denied the right to finish.

title: cruel immortality
short: In the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite, Eos asks Zeus to make Tithonus immortal but forgets to ask for youth.
body: The fullest ancient account is the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (ll. 218-238): Eos asks Zeus to make Tithonus deathless, but foolishly does not ask that he stay young. When his hair turns grey she leaves his bed though she still feeds and clothes him, and when he can no longer move she shuts him in a chamber, where his voice babbles on endlessly. Tennyson changes the story in two ways: Tithonus himself asks for immortality (l. 15), and the goddess grants it herself. 'Consumes' makes immortality a slow fire or disease eating him away.

anchor: the quiet limit of the world
title: the quiet limit of the world
short: The palace of the Dawn at the eastern edge of the world, where the sun rises.
body: Eos lives at the eastern rim of the world; in the Homeric Hymn she and Tithonus dwell 'by the streams of Ocean, at the ends of the earth' (l. 227). Tennyson's phrasing makes this a liminal place, at the 'limit' and in 'ever-silent spaces', between the human world and the divine. Tithonus is a 'white-hair'd shadow roaming like a dream', a ghost-like figure who belongs to neither world. 'Far-folded mists' and 'gleaming halls of morn' set the poem's colour scheme of grey and gold.

sources.cite: Homeric Hymn 5, To Aphrodite, ll. 218-238 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Perseus Digital Library)

title: 'Give me immortality'
short: Tithonus admits the request was his own; the goddess granted it carelessly, like the rich giving alms.
body: Unlike the Homeric Hymn, where Eos makes the request to Zeus, Tennyson makes Tithonus the petitioner, so the poem becomes a study of a wish fulfilled to the speaker's ruin. The simile 'Like wealthy men who care not how they give' catches the goddess's careless generosity: what costs her nothing costs him everything. William E. Cain, summarised in the Wikipedia article, reads Tithonus as receiving the curse of having his wish granted. The phrase 'that he seem'd / To his great heart none other than a God' shows the original fault as pride.

sources.cite: Homeric Hymn 5, To Aphrodite, ll. 218-238 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Perseus Digital Library)

title: thy strong Hours
short: The Horae, goddesses of the seasons and hours who attend the Dawn; here they take revenge by ageing him.
body: The Horae (Hours or Seasons) keep the gates of heaven in the Iliad (V.749-751) and attend the chariot of the sun and dawn in later art and poetry. RPO explains that they are 'indignant' because the gift of immortality interfered with their ordinary work: they cannot end Tithonus, so they 'beat me down and marr'd and wasted me'. The personification turns time into a group of hostile agents, and the strong verbs make ageing an act of violence.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'Tithonus', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes

title: Immortal age beside immortal youth
short: A balanced antithesis that sums up the poem's situation in one line.
body: The line repeats the end of l. 21 ('immortal youth') and sets 'Immortal age' against it with 'beside' as a fulcrum. Its symmetry mirrors the couple's fixed, endless juxtaposition: the goddess renewed each morning, the man forever older. The next phrase, 'And all I was, in ashes', breaks off the rhythm with a mid-line pause, a reminder that 'Consumes' (l. 6) is a metaphor of burning.

sources.cite: Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes
'Tithonus (poem)', Wikipedia (summarising Markley, Cain and others)

title: the silver star, thy guide
short: The morning star (Venus), which rises just before dawn and so seems to lead her.
body: The planet Venus seen before sunrise was the 'light-bringer' (Greek Phosphoros, Latin Lucifer), and so it 'guides' the Dawn. Here the star is reflected in the goddess's 'tremulous eyes that fill with tears', which places the scene at the moment before sunrise and makes her pity part of the daily cycle. Her tears are also the dew, an old association of Eos with dew and weeping (she mourns her son Memnon in later myth).

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'morning star' and 'Lucifer'

title: kindly
short: 'Kindly' here means natural, belonging to one's own kind, not simply 'kind-hearted'.
body: The older sense of 'kindly' (OED) is natural, in accordance with one's nature or kind; it comes from 'kind' meaning race or nature. Tithonus asks why anyone should wish to differ from his own natural species, mankind, which is mortal. The warmer modern sense (gentle, benevolent) is also present, so the phrase means both the race of men to whom he belongs and the race whose mortality now seems a kindness.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'kindly' adj. (natural; of one's kind)

title: goal of ordinance
short: The limit fixed by divine or natural law: death, the end-post of the human race.
body: RPO glosses the phrase as 'the limit ordained'. 'Goal' keeps its older meaning of the post or boundary marking the end of a race (like the Latin meta), so life is pictured as a course whose end is set by decree ('ordinance'). Tithonus has passed beyond it into a place where no one 'should' go. The phrase 'as is most meet for all' (most fitting) presents mortality as justice rather than loss.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'Tithonus', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'goal' n. (boundary, winning-post) and 'ordinance' n.

title: the wild team
short: The horses of the Dawn's chariot, named in the Odyssey as Lampus and Phaethon.
body: Homer names the Dawn's horses as Lampus and Phaethon ('Shining' and 'Blazing') in Odyssey XXIII.244-246, where Athena holds them back to lengthen the night for Odysseus and Penelope. Tennyson's horses 'love thee, yearning for thy yoke', and 'beat the twilight into flakes of fire', an image in which their hooves strike sparks from the dark and the first light breaks into flecks of cloud. The sensuous description of dawn makes the goddess beautiful and unreachable at the same moment she leaves him.

title: The Gods themselves cannot recall their gifts
short: A proverbial saying with Homeric roots: divine gifts cannot be refused or taken back.
body: Tithonus fears that a saying learnt long ago on earth is true. The idea goes back to Homer: Paris tells Hector that 'the glorious gifts of the gods are not to be cast aside' (Iliad III.65). In the Homeric Hymn, Aphrodite cites Tithonus's case to explain why she will not ask immortality for her own lover Anchises. The line explains why the goddess weeps: she cannot undo her gift even if she wishes to.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad III.64-66 (Greek text and A. T. Murray trans., Perseus Digital Library)
Homeric Hymn 5, To Aphrodite, ll. 218-238 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Perseus Digital Library)

anchor: if I be he that watch
title: if I be he that watch'd
short: Tithonus doubts he is still the same person who once loved her; compare Aeneas and Satan's 'how changed'.
body: The parenthesis questions whether personal identity survives such change. Similar formulas of recognition and disbelief run through epic: Aeneas sees Hector's ghost 'how changed from that Hector' (Aeneid II.274, 'quantum mutatus ab illo'), and Satan addresses Beelzebub 'If thou beest he; but O how fallen! how changed' (Paradise Lost I.84), itself an echo of Virgil. The memories that follow (ll. 53-63), of the goddess's dawn transformation and her kisses, are among the most sensuous lines Tennyson wrote, and they belong to a self he no longer recognises.

title: Apollo's song and the walls of Ilion
short: Troy's walls were said to have risen to the music of Apollo; Tithonus, a Trojan prince, heard it.
body: Tithonus was a son of Laomedon and brother of Priam (Iliad XX.237). Laomedon's walls of Troy were built by Poseidon and Apollo (Iliad VII.452-453, XXI.441-457); later tradition said they rose to the music of Apollo's lyre, as in Ovid's Heroides, where Paris promises Helen she will see Ilion's walls 'built to the music of Apollo's lyre' (XVI.179-180). Tennyson used the same legend in 'Oenone'. The simile 'like a mist rose into towers' links the city's magical birth with the dawn mists of the poem.

title: cold my wrinkled feet / Upon thy glimmering thresholds
short: Tithonus stands at the doorway between the divine east and the mortal world below.
body: The 'thresholds' and 'portals' (l. 57) of the Dawn's palace are places of passage that Tithonus can never cross. He looks down at the 'steam' rising from fields around 'the homes / Of happy men that have the power to die', the mist of the human world at dawn. The repetition of 'cold' (three times in ll. 66-67) contrasts with the 'glow' of his remembered youth. In the Homeric Hymn Eos shuts him away behind shining doors; Tennyson keeps him at the door, looking out.

anchor: grassy barrows of the happier dead
title: barrows
short: Burial mounds; the dead under them are 'happier' than the men who can still die.
body: A barrow (Old English beorg, hill, mound) is an earth mound raised over a grave, especially an ancient one. The comparative grades the human condition: men who can die are 'happy', the dead are 'happier', and the immortal Tithonus is the most wretched. The grass on the mounds suggests the earth reclaiming the body peacefully, which is what he asks for in the last lines.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'barrow' n.1

title: I earth in earth
short: An echo of the curse of Adam and the burial service: man is dust and returns to dust.
body: Tithonus asks to become what every mortal becomes: 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (Genesis 3:19), echoed in the Book of Common Prayer burial service ('earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). In the grave he will forget the goddess's 'empty courts' and her return each morning 'on thy silver wheels'. The poem ends with that return, so the cycle he cannot share is the last thing we see; the death he asks for is never granted within the poem.

sources.cite: The Bible, King James Version, Genesis 3:19
